newsitem.title: INDIA: COMMODITIES-India coffee futures trade in offing.
newsitem.headline: COMMODITIES-India coffee futures trade in offing.

text.p: Indian coffee exporters and traders say they are exploring possibilities of setting up a futures exchange in a bid to minimise risks in a volatile market.
"There's a need for trading in coffee futures in the new environment of liberalisation," said Arun Bidappa, chief executive of Karnataka Coffee Brokers' Pvt Ltd, a firm involved in coffee auctions.
"Futures trading can help minimise losses in a market that is swinging unpredictably at home and abroad," he said.
Coffee prices in international markets have fallen sharply to around 180 cents per pound at present from a high of 318 cents per pound toward the end of May.
India's domestic prices reflect global trends.
Indian coffee retail prices have stabilised at around 180 rupees per kg after rising sharply to 220 rupees per kg in June from 160 rupees per kg in the previous month.
As part of its economic reforms, India has in the last three years freed the coffee trade from five-decade-old controls, allowing growers to directly market their produce.
The state-run Coffee Board formerly collected coffee from the growers and auctioned it for both domestic and export markets.
The recently-formed Indian Coffee Trade Association, representing growers, traders and exporters, holds weekly auctions at the southern city of Bangalore.
"There's no sanctity of contracts in the absence of a proper system. So exporters and traders are planing a domestic coffee futures exchange, to begin with," Bidappa said.
A committee of exporters and traders have met twice recently to look at the possibility of setting up a futures exchange for coffee.
"The exchange will evolve a price discovery mechanism based on the market fundamentals and demand and supply situation," Bidappa said.
He said if logistics did not work out favourably for a separate exchange for coffee, it could be tagged along with some other commodity to make it viable.
Coffee growers are sceptical about the planned futures exchange because of the fears of speculation.

"We don't know anything about coffee futures. For 50 years the Coffee Board had marketed for us and private auctioneers do it now. We need to be told clearly how the futures market will work and benefit us," said M.R. Aappaya, a coffee grower.
Ashwin Shah, convenor of the committee on a coffee futures market said: "We are trying to explain to the growers the importance of a futures market. We are starting a campaign."
Government officials have made it clear that coffee growers and traders must run the futures exchange exchange themselves.
"The exchange will not be a part of any government agency," Coffee Board chairman Philipose Matthai told a recent meeting of coffee growers.
"The exchange will have to be set up by the coffee trade and industry," he said.
Coffee traders said an exchange would help growers sell their crop ahead of the harvest and traders and exporters buy stocks well in time.

They estimated the 1997/98 (October/September) coffee crop at around 220,000 tonnes, up from 180,000 tonnes in the previous year. India's coffee exports in 1996/97 (April/March) rose to 178,000 tonnes from 170,000 tonnes in the previous year.
Coffee exporters said if everything went well, futures trading in coffee could begin before the end of the year.
"It will not take much time," said Bidappa. "We have the experience of a pepper exchange to follow."
India's first global exchange in pepper futures is expected to start functioning towards the end of August.
"Everything is set for the start of the pepper exchange this month," said T. Vidyasagar, president of the Indian Pepper and Spices Trade Association.
"We have done mock trading, tested every system. We are ready. Just a few minor formalities are left," he said.
India recently announced it was allowing trading in global futures in castor oil and domestic futures in cotton and jute.
